title: Intervals

learn.summary: An interval is the distance between two notes, and it is the atom of all melody and harmony. Name intervals by counting letter names inclusively: C to E is a third, C to G a fifth. Every chord quality and every melodic leap you will ever hear reduces to a handful of these distances.

do: Do one five-minute interval session on the musictheory.net ear trainer today — ascending major 2nd, major 3rd, perfect 5th, and octave only.

children.title: Names & Quality

learn.summary: Intervals have a size (2nd through octave) and a quality: 4ths, 5ths, and octaves are "perfect"; the rest come in major and minor, where minor is one semitone smaller. In semitones: minor 3rd = 3, major 3rd = 4, perfect 4th = 5, perfect 5th = 7, octave = 12. Memorize those five numbers first.

do: On a piano app, play C up to each of: Eb, E, F, G, and C — saying "minor 3rd, major 3rd, perfect 4th, perfect 5th, octave" as you go.

children.title: Reference Songs

learn.summary: The classic hack: anchor each interval to a song opening you already know. Minor 2nd = the Jaws theme, major 2nd = Happy Birthday, perfect 4th = Here Comes the Bride, perfect 5th = Twinkle Twinkle (and the Star Wars theme), octave = Somewhere Over the Rainbow. Hear the interval, sing the song, name the distance.

do: Build your personal reference list this week: pick and write down one song you actually know for each interval from minor 2nd to octave.

children.title: Consonance & Dissonance

learn.summary: Consonant intervals (octaves, 5ths, 3rds, 6ths) sound stable; dissonant ones (2nds, 7ths, the tritone) sound tense and demand resolution. The tritone — six semitones, exactly half an octave — was nicknamed "diabolus in musica" and powers everything from Wagner to metal. Music is the managed traffic between tension and release.

do: Play C+G, then C+F#, then resolve the F# up to G on a piano app — feel the tritone's itch and its relief, and do it five times.
